The first regional project to be planned under PJM’s Order 1000 rules was the New Jersey Artificial Island transmission need (PJM Inside Lines 2021). PJM identified stability issues and requested proposals for improved operational performance in the Artificial Island area where the Salem 1 and 2 and Hope Creek 2 nuclear power plants are located. Of the 12 total transmission enhancements that made up the Artificial Island Project, 5 of the projects were planned to operate at 500 kV (345-kV double circuit) or higher with a cost allocation of 50% allocated to the region via load ratio share and 50% via solution-based DFAX method. The remaining 7 60 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. projects were planned to operate below the voltage thresholds, and 100% of the cost of these projects was to be allocated via the solution-based DFAX method, including the 3-mile 230-kV underwater cable beneath the Delaware River. This original cost allocation using DFAX and load ratio share allocated the majority of the cost of the transmission project, including nearly all the cost for the 230-kV underground transmission line, to Delmarva Power and Light, which serves customers in Delaware and Maryland. After requests for rehearing from state regulators, FERC found the DFAX method was not suitable to identify beneficiaries of stability-based upgrades because it is based on flow- based calculations. PJM proposed two alternative ex ante cost allocation approaches for identifying the beneficiaries of transmission projects that address stability-related reliability issues—the stability deviation method and the stability interface DFAX method. FERC found the stability deviation method to be just and reasonable and included the tariff provisions in the February 28, 2019, order and directed PJM to make a compliance filing with the additional provisions. A group of other state regulators and transmission owners sued and took FERC to court, arguing the commission changed its decision without proper evidence. The case went to the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia (Public Service Electric and Gas Company, Petitioner v. Federal Regulatory Commission 2021). The D.C. Appeals Court denied the petition for review of FERC orders by Public Service Electric and Gas and other petitioners, deciding FERC made the right decision in adopting the alternate cost allocation method for stability issues. In March 2020, FERC accepted PJM’s reallocation of costs for the Artificial Island Project. Using the stability deviation method, Delmarva Power and Light was allocated only 13% (PJM 2020) of the costs, compared to nearly 98% (PJM 2015b) using the DFAX methods. The 230-kV transmission line running under the Delaware River, along with the upgraded substations and new transformer, were completed in fall 2020, with the remaining upgrades completed in spring 2021 (PJM Inside Lines 2021).
